title: Process & System Monitoring Tools
summary: Reading ps, top, vmstat, and free correctly — and knowing what their numbers actually mean before you act on them.

slides.markdown:
`ps`, `top`, `vmstat`, and `free` are the first tools anyone reaches for when a box feels slow — and the fastest way to look junior in an interview is to quote a number from one of them without knowing what it actually measures.

This topic is about reading these tools correctly: what load average really encodes, why "used" memory isn't the problem it looks like, and how to tell a CPU-bound box from an I/O-bound one from the numbers alone.

slides.sectionTitle: ps: snapshotting process state from the command line
slides.markdown:
`ps` (process status) prints a **one-time snapshot** of running processes — unlike `top`, it doesn't refresh; you get the state at the moment you ran it and nothing after. That makes it the right tool for scripting (grab a PID, feed it to another command) and the wrong tool for watching something change over time.

Under the hood, `ps` is just reading `/proc/<pid>/stat` and `/proc/<pid>/status` for every process directory it finds and formatting the result — it has no special access beyond what any user process can read for processes it owns (and root can read for all of them).

The historical wrinkle worth knowing: `ps` supports three incompatible option styles — UNIX (`-ef`), BSD (`aux`), and GNU long options (`--pid`) — because of its portability history, which is why `ps aux` and `ps -ef` show almost the same information with different column layouts.

slides.sectionTitle: Code: useful ps invocations and reading their columns
slides.markdown:
```bash
$ ps aux | head -3
USER   PID %CPU %MEM    VSZ   RSS TTY   STAT START   TIME COMMAND
root     1  0.0  0.1 168000  9200 ?     Ss   09:00   0:03 /sbin/init
web    842 12.4  2.1 812400 172000 ?    Sl   09:01  14:22 node server.js
```

- **%CPU** — average CPU usage since the process started, not "right now." A process that spiked to 100% for one second an hour ago and has been idle since can still show a low %CPU here.
- **RSS** vs **VSZ** — RSS is actual physical memory resident right now; VSZ is total virtual address space reserved, which can be far larger and includes memory that's mapped but never touched.
- **STAT** — process state letters, same vocabulary as `/proc/[pid]/status` (`S` sleeping, `R` running, `D` uninterruptible, `Z` zombie), plus modifiers like `s` (session leader) and `l` (multi-threaded).

```bash
$ ps -eo pid,ppid,stat,%cpu,%mem,cmd --sort=-%cpu | head
```
sorts by CPU descending — the single most useful `ps` line for "what's eating this box right now."

slides.sectionTitle: top/htop: live, continuously refreshing process views
slides.markdown:
`top` re-runs its process scan on an interval (default 3 seconds) and redraws in place, so you watch numbers change instead of comparing separate `ps` runs by hand. It also shows a system-wide summary header — load average, CPU breakdown by category, memory and swap totals — above the per-process table.

`htop` is a friendlier reimplementation: color, mouse support, tree view of the process hierarchy (so you can see which processes are children of which), and easier sorting/filtering — same underlying `/proc` data, better UX. Neither tool has any monitoring capability the other lacks in principle; `htop` just makes common operations faster.

Both are sampling tools: whatever spiked and finished *between* two refresh intervals is invisible to them. A one-second CPU spike every 10 seconds might never appear if it happens to land between samples — this is a real blind spot, not a hypothetical one.

**Load average** — the three numbers in `uptime` or `top`'s header (e.g. `2.10, 1.85, 1.40`) — is the average number of processes **runnable or waiting** (running, ready-to-run, or in uninterruptible I/O wait) over the last 1, 5, and 15 minutes.

The number is meaningless on its own — it has to be read against the machine's CPU core count. A load average of 4 is idle-ish on a 32-core box and badly overloaded on a 2-core one. The rule of thumb: load average roughly equal to core count means the CPUs are fully but not excessively busy; well above it means processes are queuing for CPU time (or, critically, stuck in I/O wait — see the pitfall slide).

Three numbers, not one, exist so you can read a trend at a glance: 1-min lower than 15-min means load is easing; 1-min higher than 15-min means it's actively climbing right now.

slides.sectionTitle: vmstat and free: memory and CPU at a glance
slides.markdown:
`free -h` shows total, used, free, shared, buff/cache, and available memory in one line — the number that matters most for "do I actually have headroom" is **available**, not **free** (see the pitfall slide for why).

`vmstat 1` prints a rolling one-line-per-second summary with columns for processes (`r` runnable, `b` blocked), memory, swap activity (`si`/`so` — swap in/out, the two numbers you never want to see nonzero on a healthy server), I/O (`bi`/`bo` — blocks in/out), and CPU time split into `us` (user), `sy` (system/kernel), `id` (idle), and `wa` (waiting on I/O).

That `wa` column is the fastest way to distinguish "the CPU is genuinely busy" from "the CPU is idle because it's stuck waiting for disk or network" — a box can show low CPU usage in `top` and still be badly bottlenecked if `wa` is high.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: mapping "load average 8 on a 4-core box" to what's actually happening
slides.markdown:
![load average 8 meaning CPU-bound versus I/O-bound](assets/load-average-ambiguity.svg)

Load average 8 on a 4-core machine could mean two very different things: 8 processes genuinely competing for 4 CPUs (a CPU-bound problem — more cores or fewer concurrent jobs fixes it), or 4 CPUs sitting mostly idle while several processes are stuck in uninterruptible I/O wait (a storage or network problem — more CPU cores wouldn't help at all).

Load average alone can't tell these apart, because it counts both runnable *and* uninterruptible-sleep processes together — you need `vmstat`'s `wa` column or `iostat` to know which one you're actually looking at.

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: CPU-bound vs I/O-bound symptoms in these tools
slides.markdown:
| | CPU-bound | I/O-bound |
|---|---|---|
| `top`/`vmstat` CPU split | High `us`/`sy`, low `id` | Low `us`/`sy`, high `wa` |
| Process state (`ps`/`top` STAT) | Mostly `R` (running/runnable) | Mostly `D` (uninterruptible sleep) |
| Load average vs core count | Load exceeds cores, and `us`+`sy` explains it | Load exceeds cores, but CPUs look idle |
| Fix direction | More/faster CPU cores, or reduce work per request | Faster storage/network, more I/O concurrency, caching |
| Common cause | Tight compute loops, inefficient algorithms, too many concurrent CPU-heavy jobs | Slow disks, network calls, lock contention on a shared resource |

**How to tell fast:** if load average is high but `top`'s `id` (idle) percentage is also high, you're I/O-bound — the CPUs aren't the bottleneck even though the load number says something's queued.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: treating high 'used' memory as a problem without accounting for page cache
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "`free -h` shows 15GB used out of 16GB — this box is nearly out of memory."

**Why it's wrong:** Linux aggressively uses spare RAM as **page cache** — cached copies of recently-read files — because unused RAM is wasted RAM, and page cache makes repeat reads dramatically faster. That cached memory shows up as "used" in the raw numbers, but the kernel will evict it instantly and silently the moment an application actually needs that RAM. It is not memory pressure; it's a free performance optimization.

**Correct model:** look at `free`'s **available** column, not **used** or **free** — `available` is the kernel's own estimate of memory that could be given to a new process without swapping, already accounting for reclaimable cache. A box showing 15GB/16GB used but 12GB available is healthy; the same 15GB used with 1GB available is genuinely tight. Confusing these two is one of the most common false alarms in on-call rotations.

Say a report comes in: "API latency doubled in the last 10 minutes." A concrete first pass:

```bash
$ uptime
 10:14:02 up 40 days,  load average: 14.02, 9.11, 4.30   # 8-core box — climbing, above core count

$ vmstat 1 3
r  b   swpd   free   buff  cache   si   so    bi    bo   in   cs us sy id wa
1  9      0  81234  10432 512044    0    0   210   840 1200 3100  8  3  2 87

$ ps aux | awk '$8 ~ /D/'
web       5521  0.4  1.1  ...  D    10:13   0:02 /usr/bin/node worker.js
web       5522  0.3  1.1  ...  D    10:13   0:01 /usr/bin/node worker.js
```

CPU is nearly idle (`id=2`), but `wa` (I/O wait) is enormous, and several processes are parked in `D`. That combination already rules out "we need more CPU" and points squarely at storage or a slow downstream dependency.

Next, `iostat -x 1` (covered fully in the strace/debugging topic) shows one disk at 98% utilization with a queue depth of 40 — a single overloaded volume, not the CPUs, is the bottleneck. The fix direction is now obvious without guessing: move load off that disk (a different volume, a read replica) or find what's suddenly hammering it (a runaway backup job, a missing index causing full scans), not "scale up the app tier."

This five-command sequence — `uptime` → `vmstat` → `ps` by state → `iostat` — is close to the actual muscle memory a senior engineer runs before opening a single dashboard.

slides.sectionTitle: Interview framing: reasoning out loud, not reciting flags
slides.markdown:
When an interviewer says "the box is slow, walk me through your diagnosis," the strongest answers narrate a decision tree, not a list of memorized commands. Start broad (`uptime`, `top`) to classify CPU-bound vs I/O-bound vs memory-pressured, then narrow with the tool that answers the specific question that classification raises (`vmstat`'s `wa`, `iostat` per-disk, `free`'s `available`).

A weak answer lists ten tools with no order. A strong answer says: "I'd check load average against core count first to see if there's contention at all, then `vmstat` to split CPU-bound from I/O-bound, then drill into whichever one the numbers point at" — and can justify *why* each next step follows from the last one's result.

This topic and the strace/debugging topic together are meant to be recalled as one coherent story in that kind of answer, not as two separate tool lists.
